title: A Queen Who Would Not Come
sum: King Ahasuerus, ruler of 127 provinces from India to Cush, shows off his wealth for 180 days and then holds a seven-day feast for everyone in the fortress at Susa, while Queen Vashti holds a feast for the women. On the seventh day, cheerful with wine, he sends seven eunuchs to bring Vashti in her crown so that his guests can admire her beauty. She refuses.

The furious king turns to his legal experts. Memucan warns that every wife in the empire will now despise her husband, and proposes an unchangeable decree: Vashti is never to come before the king again, and her place will go to someone better. Letters go out in every script and language ordering every man to rule his house. The chapter sets the stage: a vast, lavish, easily angered court, ruled by laws and moods, and an empty place beside the king.
readings: The details fit what Greek writers and Persian remains tell of Xerxes' court: Susa's palace, the royal colors, the seven nobles, the king's banquets and his temper. On this reading the feast of the third year (483 BC) may be the council Herodotus describes before the invasion of Greece, and the chapter explains how a Jewish woman came to be queen.

Many scholars read the chapter as comedy at the empire's expense. The king who rules from India to Cush cannot get his wife to come to dinner; his advisers treat one refusal as a national emergency; and the decree meant to hush the matter announces it in every language. For Jews living under such rulers, laughter was a way of seeing that the empire's power was less solid than it looked.

views.H: A true account of a real banquet of Xerxes I in his third year, 483 BC, and of the deposing of a queen (so Baldwin and Yamauchi, with most traditional readers). The 180 days may reflect a long gathering of officials and commanders, and the 127 provinces the empire's smaller districts.
views.C: A carefully built opening of a court story: lavish lists, numbers in sevens, a drunken king and foolish advisers. Many scholars see exaggeration for comic effect and note that Herodotus names Xerxes' queen Amestris, not Vashti.
views.A: Susa's palace, the Persian royal colors, the seven noble families with access to the king (Herodotus 3.84), the king's drinking customs and the royal post all have parallels in Greek and Persian sources. No outside source names Vashti.
views.J: The rabbis fill in the story: the feast celebrated the end of Jeremiah's seventy years, the cups were the Temple vessels, Vashti was a wicked granddaughter of Nebuchadnezzar ordered to appear in nothing but her crown, and Memucan was Haman (Bavli Megillah 11b–12b).
views.X: Christian readers have often read Vashti's fall as the first link in God's hidden chain of events, and the chapter as a picture of worldly power: splendid, proud and unstable. Opinions of Vashti herself have ranged from a disobedient wife to a model of modesty.

deep.b:
The narrator never says why Vashti refused or whether she was right. Readers have filled the gap in four main ways.

Rabbinic readers were mostly harsh. The Talmud and the Targums make her a granddaughter of Nebuchadnezzar who made Jewish girls work naked on the Sabbath and was paid back measure for measure; some say she refused only because a blemish had suddenly appeared, not from modesty (Bavli Megillah 12b). On this view her fall is just, and the way is cleared for Esther.

Traditional Christian readers were divided. Some sermons treated her as a wife who wrongly defied her husband and was rightly removed; others praised her for refusing to be paraded before drunken men, while granting that the king's command was legally binding.

Feminist readers, from Elizabeth Cady Stanton's Woman's Bible (1898) to recent scholars such as Linda Day, often see Vashti as the book's first hero: a woman who would not be an object on display, and who paid the price. Some compare her with Esther: Vashti says no and is removed; Esther works inside the system and saves her people. Others reply that the book does not set them against each other, and that both act with dignity.

Literary readers such as Fox and Berlin stress the comedy. The point is less Vashti's character than the king's: his power over the world is boundless, his power over his wife is nil, and his response turns a private insult into public law. That pattern returns in chapter 3, when Haman does the same with Mordecai.

Almost all scholars identify Ahasuerus with Xerxes I (486–465 BC): the Hebrew name is the regular form of Persian Xshayarsha, the empire stretches from India to Cush as in Xerxes' own inscriptions, and Ezra 4:6 places an Ahasuerus between Darius and Artaxerxes. The dates in the book then run: the feast in his third year (483 BC, 1:3); Esther brought to the king in his seventh (479/478 BC, 2:16), after the war with Greece; Haman's lots in his twelfth (474 BC, 3:7). The Greek versions and Josephus call the king Artaxerxes, and a few older scholars preferred Artaxerxes I or II. See the variant at 1:1 and the book's opening pages.

echoes: Ezra 4:6; Daniel 6:8; 1 Samuel 15:28; 1 Chronicles 12:32; Nehemiah 1:1; Nehemiah 13:24; 1 Samuel 25:36; 2 Samuel 13:28

settings.what: The king's command to bring Vashti
settings.to: Seven eunuchs, his personal attendants, on the seventh day of the feast
settings.when: when the wine had put the king in a happy mood
settings.why: To show off the queen's beauty to the peoples and officials at the feast, a display of royal glory like the 180 days of 1:4. Knowing that the order came at the height of a drinking party, before an all-male hall, explains why readers ever since have sympathized with Vashti's refusal.
settings.readers: For Jews living under Persian or Greek rulers, the scene showed how a king's mood could become a command, and how dangerous it was to say no, which is exactly the danger Esther faces in 4:11.

settings.what: The king's question to his advisers
settings.to: The wise men who knew the times, and the seven officials of Persia and Media
settings.when: after Vashti refused, while the king was furious
settings.why: To turn a personal humiliation into a legal case: 'What does the law say?' The king hides behind law, a pattern the book repeats.
settings.readers: Jewish readers would recognize an empire run by law (dat) and by advisers, where the law could be bent to one man's anger.

settings.by: Memucan, one of the seven officials
settings.to: The king and the officials, in council
settings.when: in answer to the king's question about Vashti
settings.why: To persuade the king that Vashti's refusal threatened every husband in the empire, and to win a permanent decree removing her and giving her place to 'a neighbor of hers who is better than she.' Knowing that the speaker is a courtier playing on the king's wounded pride shows why many readers hear satire: the cure spreads the news it means to suppress.
settings.readers: For a minority who depended on such advisers' goodwill, Memucan's speech showed how quickly a court could make policy from panic, a warning that prepares them for Haman's speech in 3:8–9.
views: Some traditional readers take Memucan as a serious statesman protecting order in the royal household.
Many modern readers see a comic exaggeration: an empire-wide law to make wives respect husbands.

settings.to: Every province of the empire, in its own script, and every people, in its own language
settings.when: after the king accepted Memucan's advice
settings.why: To make law that every man rule his household, and, on the usual reading of an obscure clause, that the husband's language be spoken there. It binds every household in the empire, and it answers a problem that existed mostly in the king's pride.
views: Most commentators read the last clause as requiring a mixed household to use the husband's language (compare Nehemiah 13:24).
The Old Greek speaks instead of fear in every household, and some scholars correct the Hebrew to 'say whatever suits him'; see the variant.
settings.readers: Readers would note the machinery of empire, letters in every script and language, which Haman will soon turn against the Jews (3:12) and Mordecai will turn back (8:9).

title: Esther Becomes Queen
sum: When the king's anger cools, his young attendants propose a search for beautiful virgins from every province, to be gathered at Susa under the eunuch Hegai; the one the king likes best will replace Vashti. Among those taken is Esther, also called Hadassah, an orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, a Benjaminite descended from Kish whose family went into exile with King Jeconiah. On Mordecai's orders she keeps her people secret. Hegai favors her, and after a year of beauty treatments she goes to the king in the seventh year of his reign. He loves her more than all the others and makes her queen.

The chapter ends with a scene that seems minor: Mordecai, sitting in the king's gate, learns of a plot by two eunuchs to kill the king. Esther reports it in his name, the plotters are hanged, and the matter is written in the royal records. Mordecai gets no reward, a loose thread the story will pick up at the right moment (6:1–3).
readings: Nothing in the chapter is said to come from God. Yet everything lines up: an empty throne, a beauty search, an orphan with a guardian at court, a eunuch's favor, the king's love, a plot overheard and a reward forgotten. Jewish and Christian readers have long taken this as the book's method: God's care is shown by timing, not by miracles or speeches.

Many scholars compare Esther with Joseph and Daniel: a young Jew in a foreign court rises by beauty, wisdom and favor, and later saves others. The chapter shows how Jews could make their way in an empire, and the costs: hidden identity, life in a harem, dependence on a king's pleasure.

views.H: A historical account of how Esther became queen in Xerxes' seventh year (479/478 BC), after his return from Greece. Mordecai is a minor official at the gate whose loyalty is recorded in the royal annals.
views.C: The beauty search and Esther's rise follow folk-tale patterns (the orphan who becomes queen), and the Joseph story is a likely model. The dating of Mordecai's exile (2:6) and the rule that Persian kings married only from seven noble families raise historical questions.
views.A: Persepolis tablets and a Babylonian text name a Persian official Marduka; Greek writers describe large royal harems and eunuch keepers; Herodotus tells of Xerxes' love affairs after his return from Greece and of royal records of benefactors.
views.J: The Talmud fills Esther's silence: she kept the Sabbath by counting her maids, ate only seeds, and was taken by force; Mordecai, a member of the Sanhedrin who knew seventy languages, understood the plotters' foreign tongue (Bavli Megillah 13a–b). Her name is linked to God's hiding his face (Bavli Chullin 139b).
views.X: Christians have read Esther as a model of humility and of God's placing a person where she is needed. Some, uneasy with her marriage to a gentile king and her silence about her faith, have seen her as weak until chapter 4; the Greek Esther answers this with her prayer.

deep.b:
Esther is taken into a gentile king's harem, spends a night with him, becomes his wife, eats the king's food without recorded protest, and hides that she is a Jew. How should this be judged?

She had no choice. The verbs are passive: the women are "gathered" and Esther "was taken" (2:3, 8, 16). Many rabbinic readers stress this; the Talmud compares her to the passive ground, so that no sin is hers (Bavli Sanhedrin 74b), and says she remained Mordecai's in her heart (Bavli Megillah 13b).

She compromised. Deuteronomy forbids marrying foreigners (Deuteronomy 7:3), and Ezra and Nehemiah fought such marriages in Judah in the same period (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27). Daniel refused the king's food (Daniel 1:8). Some readers, Jewish and Christian, therefore see Esther as assimilated, a Jew who had lost her way until Mordecai's challenge in 4:13–14.

The book judges her differently. Many modern scholars, among them Fox, Levenson and Berlin, argue that the book is not concerned with these questions. Like Joseph, who married the daughter of an Egyptian priest (Genesis 41:45), Esther is a Jew of the diaspora doing what she must to survive, and her test comes in chapter 4, when she must choose whether to risk everything for her people.

The Greek answer. The Greek Esther addresses the problem directly: in her prayer she says she hates the bed of the uncircumcised, wears her crown only when she must, and has not eaten at Haman's table or drunk wine offered to idols (Addition C). That the Additions felt the need to say this shows the question was already being asked before the time of Jesus.

Mordecai is "the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a man of Benjamin" (2:5). If these are his father, grandfather and great-grandfather, and the "who" of 2:6 is Mordecai himself, he went into exile in 597 BC and would be about 120 in Xerxes' seventh year. Most interpreters therefore take the "who" as Kish, or the whole family. Many also take Shimei and Kish as famous ancestors named to link Mordecai to Saul's family: Kish was Saul's father (1 Samuel 9:1; 1 Samuel 14:51), and Shimei the Benjaminite of Saul's clan who cursed David (2 Samuel 16:5). This sets up the confrontation of 3:1: a son of Kish against an Agagite.

echoes: Genesis 41:34–43; Genesis 39:21; Daniel 1:8–9; 1 Samuel 9:1; 2 Samuel 16:5; 2 Kings 24:12–15; Deuteronomy 7:3; Deuteronomy 31:18

settings.what: The attendants' proposal of a search for a new queen, and the king's word and law that carried it out
settings.by: The young men who served the king
settings.when: after his anger at Vashti had cooled and he thought of what had been decreed against her
settings.why: To give the king a new queen and turn his mind from Vashti, by gathering beautiful virgins from every province into the harem at Susa. The king adopts it (2:4), and it goes out as 'the king's word and law' (2:8). The proposal and the edict bind royal agents in every province and the families whose daughters are taken. Knowing that it comes from courtiers anxious about the king's mood explains its haste and its scale.
settings.readers: For Jewish readers it was a reminder that the empire could take their daughters; it also starts the chain of events by which a Jewish orphan reaches the throne.

settings.what: Mordecai's order to keep her people secret (repeated at 2:20)
settings.to: Esther, as she was taken into the king's house
settings.why: To protect her by hiding that she was a Jew; no reason is given. It shapes everything that follows: her identity is the secret that will be revealed at the decisive moment (7:3–4).
settings.readers: For Jews at foreign courts, the question of when to hide and when to reveal one's people was real. The book shows both: Mordecai declares himself (3:4), Esther conceals herself until she must speak.

settings.what: Esther's report of the plot, in Mordecai's name
settings.when: after Mordecai learned that two guards planned to kill the king
settings.why: To warn the king and to credit Mordecai. The report proves the loyalty of a Jew to the king, which answers in advance Haman's charge that the Jews do not obey the king (3:8).
settings.readers: The scene told diaspora readers that loyalty to a foreign king was honorable, and that it was remembered, even if late.

title: The Lot and the Decree
sum: King Ahasuerus raises Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite above all his officials and orders everyone at the gate to bow to him. Mordecai will not, and when pressed, says only that he is a Jew. Haman, enraged, decides that killing Mordecai alone is too little: he will destroy all of Mordecai's people. In the first month he has Pur, the lot, cast to pick the day, and it comes out at Adar, eleven months away.

Haman tells the king of an unnamed people, scattered and separate, with their own laws, who do not keep the king's laws, and offers 10,000 talents of silver for a decree to destroy them. The king hands him the signet ring. On the thirteenth of Nisan letters go out in every script and language: on the thirteenth of Adar, every Jew, young and old, women and children, is to be killed and their goods plundered. The king and Haman sit down to drink, and the city of Susa is thrown into confusion.
readings: Read as the war with Amalek

The labels are deliberate: Haman is "the Agagite," Mordecai a son of Kish. Saul son of Kish spared Agag king of Amalek (1 Samuel 15), and Israel was told to remember Amalek and war with him in every generation (Exodus 17:16; Deuteronomy 25:17–19). Jewish tradition reads chapter 3 as the old enemy returning, and the reading of Deuteronomy 25:17–19 on the Sabbath before Purim keeps the link alive.
Read as a study of prejudice

Haman's speech (3:8–9) takes a true fact, that the Jews are scattered and keep their own laws, adds a lie, that they are disloyal, and closes with money. The king does not even ask who the people are. Many modern readers see here the pattern of later anti-Jewish hatred, and read the book as a warning about how genocide is set in motion by pride, bureaucracy and indifference.

views.H: A historical decree of Xerxes' twelfth year (474 BC), obtained by a powerful minister through a personal grudge. The casting of lots and the eleven-month delay are real Persian practice and real history.
views.C: The plot is driven by the story's design: an unexplained refusal, an outsized response, an enormous bribe, an irrevocable decree. Many scholars doubt that a Persian king, whose empire tolerated many peoples' laws, would order a general massacre; others note that such pogroms did happen in the ancient world.
views.A: A clay die called a puru, the Persian royal post, Persian signet seals and the huge sums of royal revenue (Herodotus 3.95) all illustrate the chapter. Greek sources describe Persian proskynesis, the full bow some Greeks refused.
views.J: The rabbis say Haman wore an idol on his garment, so that bowing to him meant idolatry (Esther Rabbah 7:5); that Haman rejoiced when the lot fell in Adar, the month Moses died, not knowing it was also the month he was born (Bavli Megillah 13b); and that Israel's half-shekel offerings had already outweighed Haman's silver (Bavli Megillah 13b).
views.X: Christians have seen in Mordecai's refusal a model of conscience before rulers (compare Daniel 3; Acts 5:29), and in Haman's decree a type of the world's hostility to God's people. Some Christian readers, with some Jewish ones, ask whether Mordecai's stand was wise as well as brave.

deep.h: Why did Mordecai refuse to bow?
deep.b:
The text gives one reason: "he was a Jew" (3:4). Bowing to great men was not forbidden: "Abraham rose and bowed low to the people of the land" (Genesis 23:7), Jacob bowed seven times to Esau (Genesis 33:3), and David bowed to Saul (1 Samuel 24:8). So readers have offered several explanations.

Religious refusal. The Midrash says Haman claimed divine honor or wore an idol, so bowing was idolatry (Esther Rabbah 7:5; compare Exodus 20:5). The Greek Additions agree: Mordecai prays that he did not bow "so as not to set a man's glory above God's" (Addition C). Many Christian readers take this view and compare Daniel's friends before Nebuchadnezzar's statue (Daniel 3).

Persian prostration. Greek writers say free Greeks refused to prostrate themselves before the Persian king, holding that such honor belonged only to gods (Herodotus 7.136). Perhaps a Jew felt the same about an official.

Ancestral enmity. A Benjaminite of Kish's line would not bow to a descendant of Agag. The Targum Sheni gives Mordecai a long speech to this effect, and many modern scholars, among them Fox and Levenson, think the labels of 2:5 and 3:1 are meant to suggest it.

Pride or rashness. Some ancient and modern readers think the book does not wholly approve: Mordecai's stand provokes a threat to every Jew, and it is Esther, not Mordecai, who must save them. Some literary readers add that the book leaves his motive half-said on purpose, so that his refusal stands simply for Jewish identity standing upright.

The Hebrew text supports none of these exclusively. What it does make clear is that Haman reads the refusal as a matter of peoples, not persons (3:6).

The chapter is precise about process. The lot is cast in the first month (3:7). Haman's request is carefully worded: he never names the people, mixes a true charge with a false one, and offers money (3:8–9). The king hands over his ring without a question (3:10–11). The scribes are summoned on a fixed date, the letters go to satraps, governors and officials, in every script and language, sealed with the king's ring (3:12), carried by runners (3:13), and published as law (3:14). Then the two men drink (3:15). Many readers find the calm of this account more chilling than any description of violence. The eleven months between decree and execution give the Jews of the empire a long time to live under the sentence, and give the story time to turn.

echoes: 1 Samuel 15:2–33; Exodus 17:8–16; Deuteronomy 25:17–19; Numbers 24:7; Genesis 39:10; Genesis 41:42; Genesis 23:7; 1 Samuel 24:8; Deuteronomy 4:27; Proverbs 16:33; Daniel 3:12

settings.what: The king's command to bow to Haman
settings.to: The king's servants in the king's gate
settings.when: when he raised Haman above all his officials (3:1)
settings.why: To honor his new favorite with the full bow of the Persian court. It binds every courtier at the gate, and it is the order Mordecai will not keep, the trigger of the whole plot.
settings.readers: Jews who served at foreign courts knew such orders. The story asks when a loyal servant of the king may refuse one, and what the refusal may cost.

settings.by: The king's servants in the king's gate
settings.when: day after day, as he refused to bow to Haman
settings.why: To press him to obey the king's command, and, when he would not, to test whether his reason would hold (3:4). Their reporting him to Haman turns a private refusal into an affair of state.
settings.readers: Diaspora readers knew the pressure of colleagues at court, and the danger that a small act of conscience could be reported upward.

settings.by: Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite
settings.when: after the lot had been cast, in Nisan of the king's twelfth year
settings.why: To win the king's consent to destroy a whole people without naming them: a true fact (scattered, with their own laws), a false charge (they do not obey the king's laws), an appeal to the king's interest, and an enormous payment. Knowing that the speaker is a man enraged by one Jew's refusal (3:5–6) exposes every word as pretext.
settings.readers: For Jews living among the nations, this was the accusation they heard in many forms; the story names it, shows where it comes from, and shows it defeated.
views: Most readers take the 10,000 talents as a payment to the treasury for the right to kill and plunder.
Some take it as an offer to make up the tax revenue lost when the Jews died.

settings.when: as he handed over his signet ring
settings.why: To hand Haman both the silver and the people, to do with as he wished. The king's indifference, never asking who the people are, makes the decree possible.
settings.readers: Readers would see that the danger lay not only in a hater but in a ruler who did not care to ask.

settings.by: Haman, in the name of King Ahasuerus, through the royal scribes
settings.to: The satraps, governors and officials of every province and people, and through them all the peoples of the empire
settings.when: the thirteenth day of the first month, Nisan, in the king's twelfth year
settings.why: To order every people in the empire to be ready to annihilate, kill and destroy every Jew, young and old, women and children, on the thirteenth of Adar, and to take their goods. It binds the officials and peoples of all 127 provinces, applies on one day, and answers no real problem: only Haman's rage.
settings.readers: For Jews scattered through the empire, the scene named their deepest fear: the empire's own machinery turned against them, with a fixed date and a published law. It also prepares them for the counter-decree (8:9–14) that uses the same machinery for their defense.

traditions.q: Mordecai would not bow to Haman (Esther 3:2). When may a Christian refuse an honor that rulers demand?
views: Christians owe honor and obedience to rulers, but must refuse what goes against the moral law or the worship of God (Catechism 2238–2242). The Greek Esther, Scripture for Catholics, gives Mordecai's reason in Addition C: he would not set a man's glory above God's.

Bowing to a ruler, like bowing to an icon, is a sign of honor, not worship, which belongs to God alone. With the Greek Esther, the Orthodox read Mordecai's refusal as a refusal of honor that claimed what is God's.

Early Friends refused to bow, take off their hats or use titles of honor to anyone, holding that such customs feed pride and that such honor belongs to no one (Robert Barclay, Apology, proposition 15, 1676). Many were fined and jailed for it.

Witnesses respect rulers and obey the law, but will not salute flags or sing national anthems, holding that such acts give the nation worship that belongs to God. Their stand led to the U.S. Supreme Court case West Virginia v. Barnette (1943), which upheld their right to refuse.

title: For a Time Like This
sum: Mordecai tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and cries out loudly in the city; Jews throughout the provinces mourn and fast. Esther, who does not yet know why, sends him clothes, which he refuses. Through the eunuch Hathach, Mordecai sends her the exact figure of Haman's silver and a copy of the decree, and tells her to go to the king and plead for her people.

Esther answers that anyone who goes to the king uninvited dies unless he holds out his gold scepter, and that she has not been called for thirty days. Mordecai replies that the palace will not save her; if she keeps silent, rescue will come to the Jews from another place, but she and her father's family will perish; and who knows whether she came to the throne for a time like this. Esther tells him to gather the Jews of Susa to fast for her three days; she and her maids will fast too; then she will go to the king against the law. "And if I perish, I perish."
readings: The chapter turns Esther from a passive figure, taken, prepared and crowned, into the one who gives the orders. At its start she obeys Mordecai; at its end he does "all that Esther had commanded him" (4:17). Many readers see this as the moment Esther becomes the heroine of her own story.

No one prays and God is not named. Yet the Jews fast and mourn, Mordecai speaks of rescue "from somewhere else," and asks "who knows?" in the language of hope used by David (2 Samuel 12:22) and the prophets. Jewish and Christian readers have heard here the book's faith: God is not named, but he is trusted.

views.H: A real exchange of messages between Mordecai and the queen, and a real fast by the Jews of Susa in Nisan of 474 BC. The law of 4:11 reflects the strict access rules of the Persian court.
views.C: The dialogue is a set-piece of the court story: the go-between, the hero's hesitation, the mentor's challenge, the decision. Many scholars see the restraint about God as the writer's deliberate choice, whether to suit a festival scroll or to make a theological point.
views.A: Herodotus describes the Median and Persian rule that no one could approach the king unannounced (1.99; 3.118–119), and the Persepolis reliefs show the king receiving visitors with a staff in hand. Mourning in sackcloth is known across the ancient Near East.
views.J: The Talmud identifies Hathach with Daniel and says the three-day fast fell over Passover, so Mordecai "passed over" the law to fast on the feast (Bavli Megillah 15a). 'Another place' became, for many readers, a hint at God, whom later Hebrew calls 'the Place.' The Fast of Esther on 13 Adar takes its name from this chapter.
views.X: Christians have read Esther's risk on her people's behalf as a picture of intercession, and some as a foreshadowing of Christ, who went to the King for his people at the cost of his life. "For a time like this" is one of the most quoted lines of the Old Testament in Christian preaching on calling and courage.

deep.b:
Mordecai's words in 4:14 are the closest the book comes to speaking of God, and readers have argued over them for centuries.

A veiled name of God. Later rabbinic Hebrew often calls God HaMakom, "the Place," and many Jewish and Christian readers hear that here: if Esther fails, God will save his people some other way. Josephus, the Targum and the Greek all make God's help more explicit in their retellings.

Another human helper. Michael Fox and others argue that "another place" is set beside "you and your father's family," so it means some other person or group. On this view Mordecai expresses confidence that the Jews will survive, a conviction rooted in faith but not a statement about God's action.

Deliberate ambiguity. Many readers think the writer wanted both meanings at once. The book never names God; it shows a world in which events nonetheless bend toward rescue, and leaves readers to name the cause. See the note on 4:14 and the book's opening pages on God's absence from the Hebrew text.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three days, and a feast set aside
deep.b: My own suggestion: the book quietly asks its readers to measure Purim against Passover. The decree is written on the thirteenth of Nisan (3:12), the eve of Passover; Esther's three-day fast, if it began then, swallowed the feast (4:16–17), a point the Talmud makes (Bavli Megillah 15a). The Exodus story is the model of rescue in which God acts openly; Esther is a rescue in which he does not appear. By having the Jews give up Passover's feasting for a fast, the book may be marking the shift from the old, visible deliverance to a hidden one, which a new feast, Purim, will celebrate. Scholars such as Gillis Gerleman have argued that Esther reworks the Exodus story in many details, and the Passover timing is widely noted; reading the fast as a deliberate 'setting aside' of Passover is my own suggestion.

echoes: Genesis 27:34; Genesis 37:34; Genesis 43:14; 2 Samuel 12:22; Joel 2:12–14; Jonah 3:5–9; Nehemiah 1:4; Ezra 8:21; Genesis 50:20

settings.to: The city of Susa, and in the end Esther
settings.when: when he learned of the decree
settings.why: To mourn and to protest in public, as close to the king's gate as sackcloth was allowed. It gets the queen's attention, which is perhaps its purpose.
settings.readers: Readers would see a Jew mourning openly in the capital, and Jews in every province doing the same (4:3): a scattered people acting as one.

settings.to: Hathach, a eunuch assigned to her
settings.when: after Mordecai refused the clothes she sent
settings.why: To find out what was wrong. It opens the only channel between the queen and Mordecai.
settings.readers: The go-between shows how cut off Esther is, even from her own family, inside the palace.

settings.what: Mordecai's message and charge to Esther
settings.when: in the city square before the king's gate, soon after the decree
settings.why: To tell her everything, prove it with the exact sum and a copy of the decree, and command her to go to the king to plead for her people. It ends the secrecy he once ordered (2:10).
settings.readers: For diaspora readers the message posed the book's question: what do Jews with access to power owe their people?

settings.what: Esther's reply: the law of the inner court
settings.why: To explain the danger: death for anyone who comes to the king uncalled, unless he holds out the scepter, and she has not been called for thirty days. It is not a refusal but an honest statement of the cost.
settings.readers: Readers would feel the force of her fear: the empire's laws bound even its queen.

settings.what: Mordecai's answer: 'for a time like this'
settings.why: To take away her hope of safety in the palace, to assure her that the Jews will be saved one way or another, to warn her that silence will cost her and her family, and to suggest that her whole rise had this purpose. It is the speech that changes her mind.
settings.readers: For Jews among the nations, the words were both comfort and charge: the people would survive, but each person placed where they could help was called to act. Readers ever since have applied them to their own moments.
views: Many readers take 'another place' and 'who knows' as veiled faith that God will save his people.
Others read them as Mordecai's conviction that the Jews will find help, without a claim about God.

settings.what: Esther's reply and the call to fast
settings.to: Mordecai, and through him all the Jews in Susa
settings.why: To call the Jews of Susa to a three-day fast for her, joined by her maids, before she goes to the king against the law, accepting that she may die. It binds the Jews of Susa for those three days and makes the whole community part of her risk.
settings.readers: For later Jews, this is the origin of the Fast of Esther before Purim, and a model of a community standing behind the one who goes to speak for it.
